title: Time, days, and schedules
goal: Telling the time the Hong Kong way (including 個字, which no Mandarin book has), naming days and dates, and putting time words in the right place — before the verb, always.
bekal: ask and tell the time: 三點半, 三點三個字
name the days of the week and dates
tell 琴日 · 今日 · 聽日 and the rest apart
put time words before the verb
make plans with a time and a place

dialogs.title: 對話 1 — What time is it?
dialogs.intro: Andi asks Wong Lai the time at a bus stop. Notice how minutes are said — the most typically Cantonese part, and the most confusing for anyone who learned from a Mandarin book.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [唔該|M4 goi1]，[而家|ji4 gaa1][幾點呀|gei2 dim2 aa3]？
lines.id: Excuse me, what time is it?
lines.literal: excuse-me, now — how-many — o'clock — huh.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [而家|Ji4 gaa1][三點半|saam1 dim2 bun3]。
lines.id: It's half past three.
lines.literal: now — three — o'clock — half.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [吓|Haa2]？[咁遲|Gam3 ci4][㗎|gaa3]？[我以為|Ngo5 ji5 wai4][得三點|dak1 saam1 dim2]。
lines.id: What? That late already? I thought it was only three.
lines.literal: huh? that — late — emphasis. I — thought — only — three — o'clock.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [你幾點|Nei5 gei2 dim2][要返工|jiu3 faan1 gung1][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: What time do you start work?
lines.literal: you — how-many — o'clock — must — return — work — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [四點|Sei3 dim2]。[仲有|Zung6 jau5][半個鐘|bun3 go3 zung1]。
lines.id: At four. There's still half an hour.
lines.literal: four — o'clock. still — have — half — classifier — hour.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [巴士|Baa1 si2][三點九|saam1 dim2 gau2][到|dou3]，[應該|jing1 goi1][趕得切|gon2 dak1 cit3]。
lines.id: The bus comes at 3:45, I should make it.
lines.literal: bus — three — o'clock — nine — arrive, should — catch — able — in-time.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [三點九|Saam1 dim2 gau2]？[即係|Zik1 hai6][幾多分|gei2 do1 fan1][呀|aa3]？
lines.id: 三點九? How many minutes is that?
lines.literal: three — o'clock — nine? that — is — how — many — minute — huh.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [三點四十五分|Saam1 dim2 sei3 sap6 ng5 fan1]。[一個字|Jat1 go3 zi6][係五分鐘|hai6 ng5 fan1 zung1]。
lines.id: 3:45. Each “字” is five minutes.
lines.literal: three — o'clock — four — ten — five — minute. one — classifier — character — is — five — minute — time.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [明白喇|Ming4 baak6 laa3]！[咁|Gam2][三點一個字|saam1 dim2 jat1 go3 zi6][係三點零五|hai6 saam1 dim2 ling4 ng5]？
lines.id: Got it! So 三點一個字 is 3:05?
lines.literal: understand — already. so — three — o'clock — one — classifier — character — is — three — o'clock — zero — five.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [啱晒|Ngaam1 saai3]！[你學得|Nei5 hok6 dak1][好快|hou2 faai3][喎|wo3]。
lines.id: Exactly! You learn fast, you know.
lines.literal: right — completely. you — learn — able — filler — fast — you-know.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [多謝|Do1 ze6]。[巴士嚟喇|Baa1 si2 lei4 laa3]，[我走先喇|ngo5 zau2 sin1 laa3]！
lines.id: Thanks. Here's the bus — I'm off!
lines.literal: thanks. bus — come — already, I — go — first — already.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [拜拜|Baai1 baai3]！[聽日見|Ting1 jat6 gin3]！
lines.id: Bye! See you tomorrow!
lines.literal: bye — bye. tomorrow — see.

notes: **[而家|ji4 gaa1] = now.** A native Cantonese word; Mandarin uses 現在. 🇭🇰 Some people write it 依家, and some say *ji4 gaa1* with the *g* almost gone — it's all the same word.
**[吓|Haa2]？ = “huh?”** — the sound you make when surprised or when you didn't catch something. ⚠️ The tone must rise (tone 2). Said flat, it becomes a different word.

**Tone-3 [咁|gam3] means “so …, that …”.** [咁遲|gam3 ci4] = that late; [咁貴|gam3 gwai3] = that expensive; [咁多|gam3 do1] = that many. Compare tone-2 [咁|gam2] from Unit 4, meaning “so, then”. Same character; only the tone tells them apart.

**[鐘|zung1] is a unit of “hours long”, [點|dim2] is “o'clock”.** [三點|saam1 dim2] = three o'clock; [三個鐘|saam1 go3 zung1] = three hours long. ⚠️ These are two completely different things, and swapping them makes your sentence nonsense. Note that 鐘 always takes the classifier 個.

**[趕得切|gon2 dak1 cit3] = make it in time.** Negative: [趕唔切|gon2 m4 cit3] = not make it in time. This verb + 得/唔 + result pattern comes up all the time: [食得晒|sik6 dak1 saai3] (can eat it all), [睇唔到|tai2 m4 dou2] (can't see it).
**[啱|ngaam1] = right, correct, just right.** [啱晒|Ngaam1 saai3] = exactly right. [啱啱|ngaam1 ngaam1] = just now. [唔啱|m4 ngaam1] = wrong, not suitable. A very common word that Mandarin doesn't have.

**[我走先|Ngo5 zau2 sin1] = “I'm off first”.** ⚠️ Watch where [先|sin1] goes: in Cantonese it comes **after** the verb, the reverse of Mandarin, which puts 先 in front. [你食先|Nei5 sik6 sin1] = you eat first; [等我諗下先|Dang2 ngo5 nam2 haa5 sin1] = let me think first.

grammars.title: Telling time: 點, 半, and 個字
body: Clock time in Cantonese is built with [點|dim2]. Minutes can be said in two systems: ordinary minutes ([分|fan1]), and the [個字|go3 zi6] system, which counts in fives. 🇭🇰 The 個字 system is far more common in conversation, and it comes from the numbers on an analog clock face.

head: Time
Cantonese
Note
rows: [三點一個字|saam1 dim2 jat1 go3 zi6]
[三點三個字|saam1 dim2 saam1 go3 zi6]

after: **The part of the day goes BEFORE the hour**: [下晝三點|haa6 zau3 saam1 dim2] = three in the afternoon. Cantonese doesn't use a.m./p.m., and 13:00–24:00 aren't used in conversation.
⚠️ **Two o'clock is always [兩點|loeng5 dim2].** This is the 二 vs 兩 rule from Unit 2: 點 is a classifier. But the minutes stay 二: [兩點二十分|loeng5 dim2 ji6 sap6 fan1].
🇭🇰 **[個字|go3 zi6] doesn't exist in Mandarin at all**, and you won't find it in any Mandarin book. It comes from the twelve numbers on a clock face — each number five minutes apart.

grammars.title: Time words go before the verb
body: This is one rule that, if you hold on to it, will save you hundreds of sentences. In Cantonese, **when** something happens is always said before **what** happens. The verb itself doesn't change at all — this is what replaces past and future tenses.

head: Cantonese
Meaning
Structure
rows: [佢琴日返咗嚟|Keoi5 kam4 jat6 faan1 zo2 lei4]。
[我三點食飯|Ngo5 saam1 dim2 sik6 faan6]。
[我星期一返工|Ngo5 sing1 kei4 jat1 faan1 gung1]。

head: Wrong
Right
rows: [我三點食飯|Ngo5 saam1 dim2 sik6 faan6]。
[佢星期一返工|Keoi5 sing1 kei4 jat1 faan1 gung1]。

after: **A time word can go in two places: before the subject or after it.** Both are correct; putting it first stresses the time a little. What's **never** correct is putting it after the verb as English does.

**With several details at once, the order is: time → place → manner → verb.** [我聽日喺屋企食飯|Ngo5 ting1 jat6 hai2 uk1 kei2 sik6 faan6] = I'll eat at home tomorrow. English orders them exactly the other way around.

⚠️ **Don't look for a past tense.** [我琴日去|Ngo5 kam4 jat6 heoi3] = I went yesterday. The verb is exactly the same as in [我聽日去|Ngo5 ting1 jat6 heoi3] (I'm going tomorrow). Only the time word is different. 🔁 The marker [咗|zo2] in Unit 9 isn't a past tense — it marks completion, which is something else.

dialogs.title: 對話 2 — Wong Lai's day
dialogs.intro: Andi asks Wong Lai about her daily routine. This whole conversation is practice in putting the time word before the verb — notice the order never changes once.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [你|Nei5][平時|ping4 si4][幾點起身|gei2 dim2 hei2 san1][㗎|gaa3]？
lines.id: What time do you usually get up?
lines.literal: you — usual — time — how-many — o'clock — rise — body — emphasis.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [七點|Cat1 dim2]。[我八點|Ngo5 baat3 dim2][要返學|jiu3 faan1 hok6]。
lines.id: At seven. At eight I have to be at school.
lines.literal: seven — o'clock. I — eight — o'clock — must — return — school.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [咁早|Gam3 zou2]！[你幾點|Nei5 gei2 dim2][食晏呀|sik6 aan3 aa3]？
lines.id: That early! What time do you have lunch?
lines.literal: that — early. you — how-many — o'clock — eat — lunch — huh.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [一點|Jat1 dim2][喺學校食|hai2 hok6 haau6 sik6]。[你呢|Nei5 ne1]？
lines.id: At one, at school. And you?
lines.literal: one — o'clock — at — school — eat. you — how-about.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我十二點半|Ngo5 sap6 ji6 dim2 bun3]。[我下晝|Ngo5 haa6 zau3][有三堂|jau5 saam1 tong4]。
lines.id: I eat at half past twelve. This afternoon I have three classes.
lines.literal: I — twelve — o'clock — half. I — afternoon — have — three — class-classifier.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [你星期幾|Nei5 sing1 kei4 gei2][最忙呀|zeoi3 mong4 aa3]？
lines.id: Which day are you busiest?
lines.literal: you — week — which — most — busy — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [星期三|Sing1 kei4 saam1]。[朝早八點|Ziu1 zou2 baat3 dim2][做到|zou6 dou3][夜晚八點|je6 maan5 baat3 dim2]。
lines.id: Wednesday. From eight in the morning until eight at night.
lines.literal: week — three. morning — eight — o'clock — work — until — evening — eight — o'clock.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [嘩|Waa4]，[十二個鐘|sap6 ji6 go3 zung1]！[你唔攰咩|Nei5 m4 gui6 me1]？
lines.id: Wow, twelve hours! Aren't you tired?
lines.literal: wow, twelve — classifier — hour. you — not — tired — really.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [梗係攰啦|Gang2 hai6 gui6 laa1]。[但係|Daan6 hai6][星期六日|sing1 kei4 luk6 jat6][我唔使返工|ngo5 m4 sai2 faan1 gung1]。
lines.id: Of course I'm tired. But I'm off on weekends.
lines.literal: of-course — is — tired — sure. but — week — six — day — I — not — need — return — work.

lines.speaker: 黃麗:
lines.text: [咁|Gam2][今個星期六|gam1 go3 sing1 kei4 luk6][得唔得閒呀|dak1 m4 dak1 haan4 aa3]？
lines.id: So, are you free this Saturday?
lines.literal: so — this — classifier — week — six — able — not — able — free — huh.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [得閒|Dak1 haan4]！[去邊度呀|Heoi3 bin1 dou6 aa3]？
lines.id: I'm free! Where to?
lines.literal: able — free. go — which — place — huh.

notes: **[平時|ping4 si4] = usually, normally.** It goes where time words go, before the verb. Another option: [通常|tung1 soeng4].

**[起身|hei2 san1] = get up; [瞓覺|fan3 gaau3] = sleep.** ⚠️ [瞓|fan3] is a native Cantonese character that Mandarin doesn't have (it uses 睡). Note also [瞓着咗|fan3 zoek6 zo2] = fall asleep, not just lie down.

**[返工|faan1 gung1] and [返學|faan1 hok6] literally mean “return to work” and “return to school”.** 🇭🇰 Cantonese uses 返 for going there, not 去 — because it's a place you go to routinely. The opposites are [收工|sau1 gung1] (finish work) and [放學|fong3 hok6] (finish school).
**[食晏|sik6 aan3] = have lunch.** [晏晝|aan3 zau3] = midday. Another form: [食晏晝|sik6 aan3 zau3]. Breakfast is [食早餐|sik6 zou2 caan1], dinner [食晚飯|sik6 maan5 faan6].
**[堂|tong4] is the classifier for lessons.** [三堂|saam1 tong4] = three classes. Don't confuse it with [堂食|tong4 sik6] from Unit 4 — same character, different meaning.
**[做到|zou6 dou3] = “work until”.** [到|dou3] after a verb marks the end point. [由…到…|jau4 … dou3 …] = from … until …: [由八點到六點|jau4 baat3 dim2 dou3 luk6 dim2].

**[得閒|dak1 haan4] = free, have time.** The opposite is [唔得閒|m4 dak1 haan4] or [忙|mong4]. 🇭🇰 [得唔得閒呀|Dak1 m4 dak1 haan4 aa3]？ is the most natural way to ask whether someone can join you — far more common than asking straight out “can you?”.

grammars.title: Days, weeks, months, dates
body: All Cantonese time units are built with numbers, with not a single special name to memorize separately — except Sunday.
after: **Dates: month + 月 + number + 號.** [三月十五號|saam1 jyut6 sap6 ng5 hou6] = March 15. Asking: [今日幾多號呀|Gam1 jat6 gei2 do1 hou6 aa3]？ and [幾月幾號呀|Gei2 jyut6 gei2 hou6 aa3]？

⚠️ **The order goes from big to small, the reverse of English**: year → month → date → day → hour. [二零二六年三月十五號星期日下晝三點|ji6 ling4 ji6 luk6 nin4 saam1 jyut6 sap6 ng5 hou6 sing1 kei4 jat6 haa6 zau3 saam1 dim2].
**Years are read digit by digit**: 2026 = [二零二六年|ji6 ling4 ji6 luk6 nin4], not “two thousand twenty-six”.

blocks.text: You'll use this daily-routine vocabulary to tell stories in Unit 12. Practice by describing your own schedule, not by memorizing the list.

blocks.title: Hong Kong hours you should know
items: 🇭🇰 **MTR rush hours**: 8:00–9:30 a.m. and 6:00–7:30 p.m. At those times, [唔該借借|M4 goi1 ze3 ze3] is the phrase you'll say most often.
**Shops open late and close late.** Most shops don't open until 11:00 and close at 10 p.m. Yum cha restaurants are the opposite: they open at six in the morning.
**[放假|fong3 gaa3] = be on holiday, be off.** [今日放假|Gam1 jat6 fong3 gaa3] = today's a day off. [請假|cing2 gaa3] = take leave. [公眾假期|gung1 zung3 gaa3 kei4] = public holiday.

blocks.text: Making plans in Cantonese almost always follows the same order: ask if they're free → name the day → name the time → name the place. Four steps, each just one short sentence.

head: Step
Sentence
Meaning
rows: [你聽日得唔得閒呀|Nei5 ting1 jat6 dak1 m4 dak1 haan4 aa3]？
[不如一齊食飯啦|Bat1 jyu4 jat1 cai4 sik6 faan6 laa1]。
How about having a meal together.
[喺邊度等呀|Hai2 bin1 dou6 dang2 aa3]？
[七點喺旺角地鐵站等|Cat1 dim2 hai2 Wong6 gok3 dei6 tit3 zaam6 dang2]。
Seven o'clock, wait at Mongkok MTR station.
[就咁話|Zau6 gam2 waa6]，[唔好遲到呀|m4 hou2 ci4 dou3 aa3]！
[唔好意思|M4 hou2 ji3 si1]，[我今日唔得閒|ngo5 gam1 jat6 m4 dak1 haan4]。
Sorry, I can't make it today.
[改第日得唔得呀|Goi2 dai6 jat6 dak1 m4 dak1 aa3]？
Can we change to another day?

blocks.title: Three lifesaving phrases about time
items: [我遲少少|Ngo5 ci4 siu2 siu2]，[等我五分鐘|dang2 ngo5 ng5 fan1 zung1]。 — I'm a little late, give me five minutes.
[我而家喺路上|Ngo5 ji4 gaa1 hai2 lou6 soeng6]。 — I'm on my way. The message most often sent on WhatsApp in Hong Kong.
[你到咗未呀|Nei5 dou3 zo2 mei6 aa3]？ — Are you there yet?

wave: Five minutes before Unit 6: write your schedule for tomorrow in Cantonese — just six lines, each a full sentence with the time before the verb. Read it out loud. Then turn it all into yesterday by changing 聽日 to 琴日, and notice that the verbs don't change at all. That's the whole Cantonese time system, in five minutes.
